resources.string: The funnel of the renal pelvis narrows into the ureter at the kidney hilum. The ureter then descends behind the peritoneum.
The ureter passes in front of the iliac vessels near the common iliac artery bifurcation as it crosses the pelvic brim.
The terminal ureter runs at a slant through the bladder wall before it opens inside. Bladder wall pressure can flatten this tunnel and limit backward flow.
This innermost lining follows the folds around the lumen and forms a barrier between urine and the tissues of the ureter wall.
Urine travels through this central space. In cross-section, folds of the relaxed mucosa can give the lumen a star-like shape.
Smooth muscle surrounds the mucosa and its supporting connective tissue. Waves of contraction propel urine toward the bladder.
This urine-facing epithelium lines the bladder. It stretches during filling while maintaining a barrier between urine and the underlying tissue.
The lining outside the trigone can form ridges when the bladder is relatively empty. The ridges flatten as the wall stretches during filling.
Each ureter empties into the bladder through its own opening. The two openings form the upper corners of the trigone.
Interwoven bundles of smooth muscle form this thick layer outside the lining and its supporting tissue. They contract to empty the bladder.
This smooth triangular area at the bladder base lies between the two ureteric openings and the internal opening of the urethra.
The internal urethral opening is the lower point of the trigone. At this point the bladder neck opens into the urethra.
The female urethra begins at this opening in the bladder neck, where the bladder cavity narrows into the urinary channel.
This passage inside the urethra carries urine from the bladder neck to the external opening. It is separate from the vaginal canal.
The female urethra opens into the vestibule, in front of and separate from the vaginal opening.
Striated muscle around the middle portion of the urethra helps close the urinary channel and contributes to voluntary control of urine flow.
This wall lies just behind the female urethra and helps support it. The urinary and vaginal passages do not connect.
